title: Can you average quiz percentages? Count the answers first
description: Two quiz percentages can look easy to combine. A tiny example and BrainiLab’s own recorded answers show why the number behind each percentage matters.
practice: Choose a topic you enjoy, then look at the answers behind your result.

sources.name: BrainiLab — first 200 completed recorded games, aggregate snapshot checked 23 October 2026
OpenStax — Introductory Statistics 2e, Measures of the Center of the Data

sections.title: A percentage needs its headcount
sections.html:
To find the percentage of answers that were correct across several quizzes, add the correct answers and divide by all the counted answers. Simply averaging the percentages gives each quiz equal weight, even when one contains many more questions.

Both calculations can answer a question. The trick is noticing which question you meant to ask.

sections.title: One short quiz, one longer quiz
sections.html:
Imagine getting 1 out of 2 answers right in one quiz: 50%. In another, you get 9 out of 10 right: 90%.

The mean of the two quiz percentages is 70%: add 50 and 90, then divide by two. Each quiz has one equal vote.

But you answered 10 out of 12 questions correctly altogether. Divide 10 by 12, then multiply by 100: about 83.3%. Here, each question has one equal vote. The longer quiz contributes more questions.

sections.title: The same distinction in BrainiLab’s data
sections.html:
Our first-200-games article reported three games with at least ten eligible recorded rounds. Their answer counts were 283/308 for Math Rush, 199/240 for World Flags and 216/320 for Science Quiz.

Across those three groups, that is 698 correct answers out of 868 counted answers: 80.4%, rounded to one decimal place. Averaging their three displayed percentages instead gives 80.8%. That gives each game group equal weight, rather than each counted answer.

These are 44 rounds from a fixed historical snapshot, not all 200 recorded games or all 90 eligible rounds. Repeat players count more than once. Math Rush skips are excluded from its answer total.

sections.title: Useful arithmetic, modest conclusions
sections.html:
The pooled figure describes those counted answers. It does not compare players fairly, measure improvement or reveal a typical visitor’s ability: the games had different questions, difficulties and rules.

Start by asking whether you want an average per quiz or a share of all answers. Then keep the original counts beside the percentages. As OpenStax’s frequency-based mean explains, the number of observations behind a value can matter.
